entry.title: Is this the best job in the natural world?

media:group.media:title: Is this the best job in the natural world?
media:group.media:description:
Matthew Jeffery has been busy gathering plants and seeds in Croatia, South Africa and Chile.
As the Expedition Botanist at Cambridge University Botanic Garden, he arguably has one of the most wonderful jobs on the planet.
But how does collecting plants help save them from extinction?
This film follows his dream role – hunting for seeds and specimens on global trips, from South Africa and Chile to Croatia – walking in Darwin’s footsteps but using modern smartphones to do things quite differently.
It shows how working with other botanic gardens helps create a ‘living collection’ that actively protects biodiversity worldwide.
The idea is simple: different gardens grow different plants, which could one day be used to bring back species lost in the wild.
Find out more here - https://www.cam.ac.uk/stories/matthew-jeffery-cambridge-expedition-botanist

entry.title: Open Research at Cambridge, featuring Professor Jennifer Gabrys.

media:group.media:title: Open Research at Cambridge, featuring Professor Jennifer Gabrys.
media:group.media:description:
For Professor Jennifer Gabrys (Department of Sociology), open research involves more than accessible outputs. Discover how she uses citizen science and open data to work with communities to tackle environmental challenges. Learn more about Open Research at the University of Cambridge: https://www.openresearch.cam.ac.uk/ Contact the team: info@openresearch.cam.ac.uk
Welcome to the first in a series of six short films by the Open Research team at the University of Cambridge. In this premiere film, we explore how embedding open research throughout the entire research lifecycle can completely transform academic study and empower communities.
We spotlight the groundbreaking work of Professor Jennifer Gabrys, Chair in Media, Culture and Environment at the Department of Sociology and head of the Planetary Praxis Research Group. The film highlights her "Citizen Sense" and "Smart Forest" projects, which showcases how digital technology and open research frameworks allow everyday citizens to become active contributors—rather than passive data points—in studying environmental issues. This film series is a collaboration between Dr Lutfi Othman from the University of Cambridge Open Research team and Colin Ramsay (Dragonlight Films). This series is funded by the University of Cambridge Enhancing Research Culture Fund, which is administered by the Research Culture team.
For more information, visit: Cambridge Open Research Website: https://www.openresearch.cam.ac.uk/ University of Cambridge Open Research Position Statement: https://www.openresearch.cam.ac.uk/cambridge/policies-frameworks/open-research-position-statement
Planetary Praxis Research Group: https://planetarypraxis.org/ Professor Jennifer Gabrys’ website: https://www.jennifergabrys.net/
Look out for the next 5 films in this series showcasing open research across the University of Cambridge.

entry.title: Is this the earliest evidence of a fatal wooden spear attack on a human ancestor?

media:group.media:title: Is this the earliest evidence of a fatal wooden spear attack on a human ancestor?
media:group.media:description:
A circular hole in a 75,000-year-old scapula/shoulder blade suggests lethal conflict involving sharpened wooden spears among Neanderthals in the Middle East. The remains also show evidence of a brutal facial injury at least a year before death, meaning the Neanderthal was likely cared for prior to dying violently. Watch Dr Emma Pomeroy discuss the violence and compassion captured by the remains of a new Neanderthal discovery: Shanidar A.

entry.title: Crops for the future – How AI is helping plants fight against parasitic worms

media:group.media:title: Crops for the future – How AI is helping plants fight against parasitic worms
media:group.media:description:
Plant-parasitic nematodes are a major threat to global food security, causing billions of pounds of crop losses every year. These microscopic, worm-like creatures infect the roots of every major food crop, draining vital resources and reducing harvests.
Traditionally, identifying which plants have natural genetic resistance to these pests has been painstakingly slow. But researchers at the University of Cambridge’s Crop Science Centre have developed a method using 3D-printed robots and cutting-edge AI to massively accelerate this work.
By automating how they image and analyse nematode-infected plants, the team can now image and analyse around 1,000 plants an hour – a huge increase from the previous limit of just 90 plants a day.
The AI models identify nematodes with a high level of accuracy, allowing researchers to track the entire life cycle of the parasite and pinpoint specific plant genes that govern resistance. The ultimate goal of this research is to identify resistance genes that allow for the development of naturally resilient crops and support a future of sustainable farming across the globe.
With thanks to Graham CopeKoga at the Cambridge Philosophical Society for producing this video – and to Sebastian Eves-van den Akker and his group including Siyuan Wei, Jie Zhou, Olaf Kranse, Unnati Sonawala, Paul Goodman and George Harpum for their support in documenting their work.

entry.title: What can a 194-year-old tortoise teach us about ageing?

media:group.media:title: What can a 194-year-old tortoise teach us about ageing?
media:group.media:description:
What can a 194-year-old tortoise teach us about ageing? 🐢🧬
This is Jonathan, the world’s oldest living giant tortoise and land animal.
Scientists, including Dr Justin Gerlach from Peterhouse, studied Jonathan’s DNA to find out how his body has kept going for almost two centuries.
The research points not only to unusual genetic variants, but to the way his genes are switched on and off, including processes involved in DNA repair and metabolism.
These findings could help us better understand the biological processes that shape ageing and longevity across species.
Learn more about this new study: https://www.cam.ac.uk/research/news/genetic-analysis-of-the-worlds-oldest-land-animal-reveals-secret-of-living-194-years

entry.title: How to win an 18 boat rowing race

media:group.media:title: How to win an 18 boat rowing race
media:group.media:description:
Want to get involved in rowing at Cambridge?
Most of the college clubs have boats that cater to people at every level. Two of the main events in the calendar year are the Lent and May bumps organised by the Cambridge University Combined Boat Clubs (CUCBC). These pit up to 18 boats at a time against each other in a series of races down the narrow River Cam.
@yanr4n takes part in rowing with her college club @emmanuelcambridge and explains how these races actually work.
If you would like to learn more about bumps and recent results, visit this website: https://www.cucbc.org/
Thank you to @LaGrosseBelette and @tahmidazam639 for allowing them to use some of their race footage
